code.title: Lost updates: unsafe ++ versus Interlocked

followUps:
Run it many times under stress and look for wrong results, because a race is a timing bug that hides on a single try. Hammer the code with many threads and iterations, compare against the expected answer, and repeat thousands of times. Example: 8 threads each add 100000 times; the total must be 800000, and any smaller number proves lost updates.

Help it along with Thread.Yield() or random sleeps to shake out interleavings, run on ARM and with many cores, and use tools such as a thread sanitizer or Coyote. A passing test never proves safety; it only raises confidence.

code.title: lock is Monitor.Enter/Exit in a finally block

followUps:
A lock convoy is a pile-up where many threads queue for one hot lock and each hand-off costs a context switch, so throughput collapses. Threads wake, find the lock taken again, and sleep again, so the lock is busy but little real work gets done.

It appears when a lock is held briefly but requested very often, or when the holder gets preempted inside the critical section. Fixes: shrink the critical section, split the lock (per shard), use Interlocked or thread-local data, or reduce how often threads touch the shared state.

.NET 9 adds a dedicated System.Threading.Lock type, and lock on a variable of that type uses its own EnterScope method instead of Monitor. It is a little faster and states the intent clearly.

private readonly Lock gate = new();
lock (gate) { total++; }   // uses gate.EnterScope()

Rules stay the same: short sections, no await inside. Caution: locking a Lock object through Monitor directly, or casting it to object, does not use the new path.

code.title: Deadlock prevention with a global lock order

followUps:
Livelock is when threads are not blocked but keep reacting to each other and make no progress. Two people in a corridor who both step aside the same way forever are the picture.

In code, two threads each take a lock, fail to get the second via TryEnter, release the first, and retry in perfect step, forever. CPU is busy while nothing completes. Fix by adding random backoff (jitter), a fixed lock order, or a priority so that one side always wins. Deadlock burns no CPU; livelock does.

code.title: Interlocked CAS loop, and a lock for two variables

followUps:
Push builds a new node and uses compare-and-swap on the head, retrying if another thread changed the head first. No lock is held, so a stalled thread cannot block others.

do {
  old = Volatile.Read(ref head);
  node.Next = old;
} while (Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref head, node, old) != old);

Example: head is A; two threads push B and C. One CAS wins (head becomes B), the other sees head changed, relinks to B and retries. Cost is O(1) amortized, O(1) space per push. Pop is harder because of the ABA problem; .NET's GC makes the push/pop pair safe because a node cannot be reused while referenced.

code.title: volatile stop flag and Volatile.Read/Write

followUps:
Because the compiler or CPU could reorder the writes, another thread could see the object reference before its fields were fully set. The classic pattern checks if (instance == null), locks, checks again and assigns, but the assignment could become visible before the constructor finished.

Another thread then skips the lock because the reference is non-null and uses a half-built object. Making the field volatile gives the write release semantics, so construction completes first. In modern C#, just use Lazy<T> or a static initialiser, which are correct and simpler.

code.title: SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync throttling to 3 at a time

followUps:
SemaphoreSlim does not remember which thread holds it, so a method that waits on it and then calls itself (or another method that waits) blocks on its own permit and deadlocks. With a count of 1, the second Wait from the same thread simply waits forever for a release that only that same thread can make.

await sem.WaitAsync();
await Recurse();   // calls WaitAsync again: stuck

Fixes: restructure so only the outer method takes the semaphore and inner helpers assume it is held, pass a flag, or use a reentrant Monitor when no await is involved.

code.title: ConcurrentDictionary.AddOrUpdate counting

followUps:
Use ImmutableDictionary when reads vastly outnumber writes and you want consistent snapshots without locks. A reader grabs the reference and enjoys a frozen, unchanging view, so enumeration and multi-key reads are always consistent.

Writes create a new version sharing most structure, costing O(log n) each and extra allocation, and concurrent writers need a CAS loop or ImmutableInterlocked.AddOrUpdate. For write-heavy or hot-path counters, ConcurrentDictionary is faster. Example: a config table updated once a minute and read a million times a second fits the immutable one.

Complete the writer, let the readers drain what is left, and wait for the reader tasks to finish. Complete() tells the channel no more items will come; readers using ReadAllAsync keep receiving queued items and then exit their loop on their own.

writer.Complete();           // producers done
await Task.WhenAll(consumers); // drain
await reader.Completion;     // fully finished

For a faulted pipeline call Complete(exception) so readers see the error. For cancellation, pass a CancellationToken to the reads and still complete the writer so nothing waits forever. Multi-stage pipelines complete each stage's writer when the previous stage's readers finish.

code.title: Parallel.For with thread-local sums

followUps:
Partitioner.Create splits the range into chunks so each worker gets a block of indexes instead of one at a time, which cuts scheduling overhead for tiny loop bodies. Without it, Parallel.For with a trivial body spends more time handing out work than doing it.

Parallel.ForEach(Partitioner.Create(0, n, 10000), range => {
  for (int i = range.Item1; i < range.Item2; i++) Work(i);
});

With n = 1,000,000 and chunk 10,000 there are only 100 delegate calls instead of a million. Too large a chunk hurts load balancing when iterations vary in cost.

code.title: Thread vs pool Task vs LongRunning task

followUps:
The pool slowly runs out of threads, queued work waits, and the whole app looks frozen (thread-pool starvation). The pool starts with about one thread per core and adds new ones only slowly (roughly one or two per second) when all are busy.

Example: 100 requests each block a pool thread for 5 seconds with 8 cores; most requests wait for new threads to be injected, so latency spikes far beyond 5 seconds, and even timers and continuations are delayed. Fix: make the blocking work async, use a dedicated thread or LongRunning task, limit concurrency, and never block on .Result inside the pool.

code.title: Print foo/bar alternately with two semaphores

followUps:
Use a Monitor with a shared turn variable and call Wait until it is your turn, then PulseAll to wake the other thread. PulseAll is safer than Pulse because only one thread can be waiting here and you recheck the condition anyway.

lock (g) {
  while (!fooTurn) Monitor.Wait(g);
  Print("foo"); fooTurn = false;
  Monitor.PulseAll(g);
}

Bar mirrors it with while (fooTurn) and sets fooTurn = true. The while loop (not if) guards against spurious or early wakeups. Cost is O(n) time for n prints and O(1) space.

code.title: False sharing: adjacent vs padded counters

followUps:
Measure it: the same work runs much slower with several threads than with one, even though they share no data. Compare timings of adjacent per-thread slots against padded ones; a large gap (often 2x to 10x) points at false sharing.

Tools help: hardware counters such as cache-miss and cache-line contention (perf c2c on Linux, VTune on Intel) show lines bouncing between cores. In this module's program, 2 threads with 2,000,000 increments each get the same total (4,000,000) either way; only the time differs. Confirm by padding the data to 128 bytes and re-measuring.

code.title: Copy-on-write immutable snapshot

followUps:
For an iterator it means that enumerating while another thread changes the collection must not crash or return corrupt data. Most ordinary collections are not safe: changing a List while enumerating it throws InvalidOperationException.

Thread-safe collections choose different promises. ConcurrentDictionary enumeration never throws, but it is not a snapshot, so you may see some updates made during the loop and miss others. Immutable collections enumerate a true frozen snapshot. Example: copy with ToArray() (a consistent snapshot under all locks) before a long iteration if you need a stable view.

code.title: Simulating the 2-out-of-2000 interleaving

followUps:
volatile would not change the answer: count can still be anywhere from 2 to 2000. Volatile only guarantees that each read sees the latest write and that reads and writes are not reordered across it. It does not make count++ atomic, which is still a read, an add and a write.

Both threads can volatile-read 5, add 1 and both volatile-write 6, losing one increment. The fix is Interlocked.Increment(ref count), which gives exactly 2000, or a lock. Use volatile for flags and published references, not counters.
